title: Privileging the Privileged
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Writing at Mutually Assured Instruction, the author builds an extended analogy between pure-inquiry-based learning and cryptocurrency speculation, prompted by a podcast interview about crypto's harms. Both, the piece argues, are hypothetical constructs that disproportionately reward people who already hold an advantage (background knowledge or existing wealth) while leaving novices exposed to loss. The author is careful to distinguish this from inquiry learning as a method entirely, but argues its most doctrinaire advocates ignore how much prior knowledge unguided discovery actually requires to work safely. The piece concludes that because both systems leave too much to chance, instruction that is known to work reliably should be the default rather than a gamble.
points: Draws a sustained analogy between pure-inquiry learning and cryptocurrency: both are hypothetical constructs that privilege those already advantaged.
Argues novices lacking background knowledge are harmed, not helped, by discovery-based approaches, mirroring how under-resourced investors are harmed by crypto's volatility.
Distinguishes the critique from inquiry learning as a method altogether, targeting its most absolutist advocates instead.
Concludes that because both systems leave outcomes to chance, instruction with a known track record should be preferred over discovery for novices.
quotes: As Ben spoke throughout this podcast he referred to the way in which bad actors endorsed a product (which is really a nothing) that targeted disadvantaged individuals and despite promises of great success that would come from the investment, the outcome for almost everyone other than the most privileged, was loss.

Inquiry learning for novices is likely to lead students to have poor literacy, numeracy and contextual background knowledge, all of which they need to interact meaningfully with the world. Cryptocurrency is an unregulated form of money of which the value can cycle violently based on the tweets of trillionaires.

Have you met anyone who gets all of their news from Facebook and "does their own research"... pure discovery is fraught with danger for any humans who lack the depth of knowledge required to analyse sources and ask questions worth inquiring about.
At the end of the day, there's too much chance involved on both sides. Learning shouldn't be left to chance.
That's not to say that inquiry learning cannot work. It absolutely can. It is just that its most staunch advocates will tell you that students need to discover things for themselves.
